title: End-of-Year Thoughts on PostgreSQL (2025)
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
I’m a developer advocate at MongoDB, a database that feels like a well-designed embedded document: multiple clouds and diverse workloads, all neatly nested within one unified data platform, one managed service, and one company. Meanwhile, I'm watching PostgreSQL’s growing popularity, which reminds me of a well-normalized one-to-many relationship: one core engine and community branching into an ecosystem of forks, extensions, architectures, and providers.

How will it grow in 2026? I'm sure the community will stay strong and united, but what about the fragmented ecosystem around it? More extensions, companies, forks, and services? Or perhaps some consolidation or more acquisitions? All of this is fascinating, but it’s also a bit unclear where it’s headed.

Here is what I observed this year around PostgreSQL—a lot happened in 2025.

PostgreSQL 18: Improvements in I/O and Queries

PostgreSQL 18 brings tangible improvements. While the developer community seems to favor uuid7() as the best feature—which in my opinion is nice to have but easy to work around, as the application often generates UUIDs—I see some more significant moves:

  • Asynchronous I/O using io_uring on Linux. PostgreSQL finally acknowledges that to run enterprise workloads, it must optimize disk access at the database level rather than relying solely on operating system abstractions. Note that direct I/O is still a debug parameter, but it is no longer treated as an "oracleism" that PostgreSQL doesn't want.
  • More query planner improvements to handle less-than-optimal queries. For a long time, PostgreSQL’s position was that if you could rewrite your SQL to obtain a better execution plan, you should, rather than expect more transformations in the query planner. But as PostgreSQL becomes more widely adopted in enterprises—where not all queries can be modified—this stance has evolved. PostgreSQL now supports index skip scans when there is no condition on the first column of an index key (this can happen when an application designed for multi-tenancy is used for a single tenant). It also supports virtually generated columns to transparently compute expressions that could otherwise be written directly in the query. In addition, it can remove unnecessary joins, such as self-joins, which often appear when querying through views or with generated SQL.

Text and Vector Search: More and More Extensions

Extensions can add functions and indexes for advanced search features, avoiding the need for additional purpose-built databases. However, it remains fragmented, with many extensions doing the job: pg_search (ParadeDB) or pg_textsearch (TigerData) for BM25 scoring? pgvector or pgvectorscale on top of it? There's also alternative vector indexing like DiskANN in HorizonDB. It's commonly known that you can do everything with PostgreSQL, but which PostgreSQL?

Architecture: Disaggregated or Local Storage?

There are two different visions for the architecture of PostgreSQL cloud services.

Disaggregated camp (agility, scale-to-zero):

  • Databricks acquired Neon. Serverless Postgres with instant branching and provisioning, favoring disaggregated storage. Integrated as a managed serverless Postgres unified with the Databricks lakehouse, by renaming it lakebase.
  • Azure HorizonDB preview announced at Microsoft Ignite in November 2025. Microsoft's PostgreSQL-compatible service with disaggregated storage, scale-out compute, and built-in AI capabilities like advanced DiskANN vector indexes. There's one more alternative to Amazon Aurora and Google AlloyDB.

Local/performance camp (raw throughput):

  • PlanetScale Postgres reached general availability in September. After MySQL success, PlanetScale offers PostgreSQL with local NVMe disks for predictable performance. They also announced Neki, their sharding solution for PostgreSQL that brings Vitess to PostgreSQL.
  • Supabase continued advancing OrioleDB, a new storage engine acquired earlier, bringing improvements like better concurrency and WAL efficiency to standard Postgres instances. They also have their sharding solution, Multigres, another Vitess for PostgreSQL.

Scalability: Distributed or Sharding?

  • YugabyteDB significantly enhanced PostgreSQL compatibility in 2025, rebasing on PostgreSQL 15 and adding features such as generated columns, foreign keys on partitioned tables, and improved query optimization. They also added features that may no be so important for a distributed database, but are for PostgreSQL compatibility, like transactional DDL and advisory locks.
  • With Aurora DSQL, AWS pushed further into distributed, with less PostgreSQL compatibility but an architecture optimized for their cloud.
  • The old idea of sharding and replicas continues to gain traction, as Citus is not alone: Aurora Limitless for AWS, Nile for multi-tenant SaaS, PlanetScale's Neki, and Supabase's multigres, PgEdge, PgDog...

DocumentDB extension

Given MongoDB’s growing popularity, Microsoft has open-sourced its PostgreSQL-based emulation as DocumentDB, and several companies have announced plans to contribute, including Microsoft, AWS, Google, Snowflake, Supabase, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, SingleStore, Rippling, and Ubicloud.

What will it mean in practice? Will CockroachDB really integrate a PostgreSQL extension into its Go-based database? Will AWS migrate its existing DocumentDB offering to this new, PostgreSQL-based DocumentDB, even though they’re different products and AWS DocumentDB still has new features on its roadmap? And will Google seriously invest in an extension that ultimately powers Microsoft’s Cosmos DB when they have a MongoDB emulation on Firebase?

Market Dynamics: Analytics Giants Enter OLTP

Analytics players moved into transactional via Postgres acquisitions:

  • Databricks acquired Neon: Serverless Postgres, integrated for lakehouse unification with OLTP.
  • Snowflake acquired Crunchy Data: Launched Snowflake Postgres, focusing on enterprise security, compliance, cloud integration.

Deeper federation and connectors also emerged to enable querying PostgreSQL from analytic solutions such as Snowflake, Databricks, ClickHouse (via PeerDB), and DuckDB.

Still, OLTP is different from Analytics. To compete with Oracle Database or SQL Server for relational databases, or with MongoDB for document databases, PostgreSQL needs stronger high availability, which is not yet built in. Neon can start instances quickly, but it's still a single-node solution for consistent read-write transactions, and running PostgreSQL in Kubernetes or calling it Cloud-Native doesn't scale it horizontally when a single pod is a single point of failure.

Looking Ahead to 2026

Will the major cloud providers’ forks and acquisitions drive consolidation or further fragmentation? On one side, analytics giants are targeting migrations from Oracle, Db2, or SQL Server with unified data platforms. On the other hand, many enterprises still favor pure Postgres compatibility for more freedom. Distributed SQL promises the highest resilience, yet sharding with read replicas is still considered for multi-tenancy. Meanwhile, open-source storage innovations—from vacuum improvements to OrioleDB and complete storage engine rewrites—could meaningfully shift the balance, but require forks that add many hooks into PostgreSQL code.

Looking ahead to 2026, will the momentum favor more unified extension and storage layers, or deepen the split between disaggregated serverless architectures and high-performance local deployments? AI workloads will likely set the pace: should vector search live in the core engine, in extensions, or on specialized replicas? With investor focus locked on AI, is the relational or document model the best fit for vibe coding?

The innovation is exciting, but enterprises transitioning away from Oracle Database, Db2, or SQL Server still need both a clear modernization path and a well-defined target destination. We can confirm that “PostgreSQL can do it” or is at least “good enough for many workloads”, but the real challenge begins when you ask: which PostgreSQL?

Another highlight in the PostgreSQL area this year was Denis Magda 's book, which covers PostgreSQL and its major extensions in one place, to help developers better navigate this complex ecosystem.
